hints: Start by picturing the starting DNA as a double helix - what must happen to the two strands before either can be copied?
Think about what breaks hydrogen bonds between bases without breaking the strands themselves, and what temperature does this.
Once you have single strands, how does DNA polymerase know exactly where to start copying? Think about short starter pieces.
Recall how those starter pieces attach - what type of bonding is involved and what temperature favours it?
Now think about the building stage - what enzyme builds the new strand and what raw materials does it need?
Consider why a normal human enzyme would be destroyed in this process, and what special polymerase from bacteria solves this.
Think about the temperature for the building stage and why it is close to the optimum for that bacterial enzyme.
Finish by thinking about what happens after one copy is made - how do you get from 2 copies to 4, 8, 16 and millions?
walkthrough:
Separate the strands - denaturation**
Think of double-stranded DNA as a zip that must be undone before copying. Heating to $94-95^\circ\text{C}$ breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases, so the helix denatures into two single strands. These single strands will both act as templates.

Attach the starters - annealing**
DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing, it needs a primer. You add short single-stranded DNA primers and cool to $55-65^\circ\text{C}$. At this lower temperature the primers can anneal - that means they bind by complementary base pairing (A to T, C to G) to their matching sequences flanking the target DNA.

Build the copies - extension**
Now heat slightly to $70-75^\circ\text{C}$. Thermostable Taq polymerase, originally from hot-spring bacteria, works at its optimum here. It reads each template strand and adds free deoxyribonucleotides one by one, forming phosphodiester bonds to build two new complementary strands.

Repeat automatically for exponential gain**
Each new double-stranded molecule is then heated again to denature, so the three-stage cycle repeats. Because Taq polymerase is thermostable it is not denatured at $94^\circ\text{C}$ and does not need replacing. The whole process is automated in a thermal cycler, so DNA doubles each cycle to clone and amplify millions of copies.

Final answer: DNA is heated to $94-95^\circ\text{C}$ to denature it to ssDNA. Mixture is cooled to $55-65^\circ\text{C}$ and DNA primers anneal by complementary base pairing to sample DNA. Heated to $70-75^\circ\text{C}$ where thermostable Taq DNA polymerase adds free nucleotides to build new strands. New strands are denatured and the cycle is repeated many times automatically, without replacing the enzyme.

hints: Think about the old way of getting factor VIII - from donated human blood. What limits how much you can get?
Now picture putting the human gene into fast-growing bacteria or hamster cells in a fermenter - what does this allow for supply?
Focus on the protein itself - if the gene has the same base sequence, what will be true about the amino acid sequence?
Link that identical sequence to the immune system - why would the body accept this protein but reject an animal protein?
Think about side effects and allergic reactions when a drug exactly matches the natural human protein.
Compare blood donation with a sterile fermenter - what infection risk is removed when no human donors are involved?
Finally, think about downstream processing - why is it simpler to purify one protein made by engineered cells than from blood plasma?
walkthrough:
Solve the supply problem**
Factor VIII for haemophilia and adenosine deaminase for SCID used to come from human blood or tissues, which are scarce. By inserting the human gene into a bacterial host, hamster cell host or insect larva cells grown in fermenters, you can produce much larger quantities continuously and reliably.

Make an exact human copy**
Because you transfer the exact human coding sequence, transcription and translation produce a protein with the same amino acid sequence as the natural human protein. The shape and function are therefore identical to the patient's own protein.

Gain immune safety**
The immune system recognises foreign proteins as antigens. Since the recombinant protein is identical to human protein, it does not trigger an immune response. That also means fewer side effects compared with animal-derived or slightly different proteins.

Remove infection risk and improve purity**
Blood-derived products carry risk of transferring pathogens such as HIV and hepatitis. Recombinant production in controlled sterile culture removes that donor-disease risk. It is also easier to obtain a purified product because the host cells secrete essentially one desired protein rather than the complex mixture found in plasma.

Final answer: Recombinant techniques allow production of large quantities using bacterial / hamster cell / insect larva cell hosts. Product has same amino acid sequence as human protein so is exactly the same as human protein, causing no immune response and no side effects. No risk of transfer of disease from donors and purified product is easier to obtain.
